q: Guacamole is mostly mashed-up what?
fact: Guacamole is an avocado-based dip first developed in Mexico; its name means 'avocado sauce'.

q: Marzipan is a sweet paste made from sugar and what?
fact: Marzipan is a confection made mainly of sugar and ground almonds.

q: Tofu is made by curdling milk from which bean?
fact: Tofu is pressed curds of coagulated soy milk.

q: The dip hummus is mainly made from mashed what?
fact: Hummus is cooked, mashed chickpeas blended with tahini, lemon juice and garlic.

q: The pricey spice saffron comes from the stigmas of which flower?
fact: Saffron threads are the dried stigmas of Crocus sativus, picked by hand, which is why it costs so much.

q: Vanilla flavouring comes from the seed pods of which type of plant?
fact: Vanilla is a spice from orchids of the genus Vanilla.

q: Tequila is made from which plant?
fact: Tequila is distilled from the blue agave plant, mainly around the Mexican town of Tequila.

q: Botanically speaking, what is a tomato?
fact: A tomato is the edible berry of the tomato plant, even though we cook it like a vegetable.

q: Which of these is botanically a true berry?
fact: Bananas count as true berries; strawberries and raspberries do not, botanically.

q: On a cashew tree, the nut hangs from the end of what?
fact: The cashew drupe grows at the end of the cashew apple, a swollen stalk.

q: Botanically, peanuts are closer to which group?
fact: Peanuts are legumes whose pods develop underground.

q: Coffee beans are actually the seeds of what?
fact: Coffee beans are seeds from the fruits ('cherries') of the Coffea plant.

q: Which country grows the most coffee in the world?
fact: Brazil produced about 31% of the world's coffee in 2023 and has led production since the 1850s.

q: Green, black and white tea all come from which plant?
fact: They differ in how the leaves are processed, not in the plant: all are Camellia sinensis.

q: What makes popcorn kernels explode?
fact: Heated moisture in the kernel becomes steam until the pressure bursts the hull.

q: Kiwifruit originally came from which country?
fact: Kiwifruit is native to central and eastern China; New Zealand started growing it commercially in the early 1900s.

q: Potatoes were first domesticated in which region?
fact: Potatoes were domesticated 7,000-10,000 years ago around Peru and Bolivia, then reached Europe in the 1500s.

q: Kombucha is a fizzy drink made by fermenting what?
fact: Kombucha is sugared tea fermented with a culture of bacteria and yeast (a SCOBY).

q: Mead is an alcoholic drink made from fermented what?
fact: Mead is honey fermented with water, sometimes with fruit or spices.

q: In Italian, what does the pasta name 'farfalle' mean?
fact: Farfalle comes from the Italian word for butterflies.

q: The Italian dessert tiramisu translates roughly to what?
fact: Tiramisu comes from 'tirami su', meaning 'pick me up' or 'cheer me up'.

q: Cabbage, broccoli, kale and cauliflower are all what?
fact: They are cultivars of the single species Brassica oleracea, bred into very different shapes.

q: Which country makes most of the world's maple syrup?
fact: Canada produces more than 75 percent of the world's maple syrup, mostly in Quebec.

q: Which part of the rhubarb plant is safe to eat?
fact: The stalks are edible; the leaves are poisonous because of oxalic acid.

q: Kimchi, a spicy fermented side dish, comes from which country?
fact: Kimchi is a traditional Korean dish of salted, fermented vegetables, most often cabbage or radish.

q: Japanese sake is brewed from fermented what?
fact: Sake is a Japanese alcoholic drink made by fermenting polished rice.

q: Feta, the crumbly brined cheese, comes from which country?
fact: Feta is a Greek white brined cheese made from sheep's milk or a sheep and goat milk mix.

q: Chocolate is made from the beans of which tree?
fact: Cocoa beans are the dried, fermented seeds of Theobroma cacao, the basis of chocolate.

q: Which chemical makes chili peppers taste hot?
fact: Capsaicin is the main active component of chili peppers and causes the burning sensation.

q: Which of these can last almost forever if stored well?
fact: Honey's sugar and acidity stop most microbes growing, so it does not spoil when properly stored.

q: Which fish gives Worcestershire sauce its savoury punch?
fact: Worcestershire sauce is made with vinegar, anchovies, tamarind, garlic, onions and molasses.

q: Nutella is a chocolate spread made with which nut?
fact: Nutella is a sweetened hazelnut cocoa spread made by the Italian company Ferrero.

q: Bubble tea was first invented in which country?
fact: Bubble tea originated in Taiwan in the 1980s.

q: Poutine, fries with cheese curds and gravy, comes from which country?
fact: Poutine emerged in Quebec, Canada, in the 1950s.

q: Paella is a famous rice dish from which country?
fact: Paella comes from the Valencia region of Spain.

q: A mushroom is the fruiting body of which kind of living thing?
fact: Mushrooms are the spore-bearing fruiting bodies of fungi, not plants.

q: What is the largest animal known ever to have lived?
fact: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever existed.

q: Which is the fastest land animal?
fact: Cheetahs can run about 93-104 km/h (58-65 mph).

q: How many neck vertebrae does a giraffe have?
fact: Just like humans, giraffes have seven neck vertebrae; each one is just hugely long.

q: Which is the only mammal capable of true, sustained flight?
fact: Bats are the only mammals capable of true and sustained flight; flying squirrels only glide.

q: What is a baby kangaroo called?
fact: Young kangaroos are called joeys and live in the pouch for months.

q: In seahorses, which parent carries the babies?
fact: The female deposits eggs in the male's brood pouch, and he gives birth to the fry.

q: Flamingos are pink because of what?
fact: Their pink colour comes from carotenoids in their diet of plankton.

q: The axolotl is famous for being able to regrow what?
fact: Axolotls can regrow lost limbs and tails over a few months.

q: Which furry Australian mammal lays eggs?
fact: The platypus is a monotreme, a mammal that lays eggs instead of giving birth to live young.

q: A narwhal's long 'horn' is actually what?
fact: The narwhal's spiralled tusk is a canine tooth growing through the upper lip.

q: Which land mammal is pregnant the longest?
fact: Elephant pregnancy lasts 21.5 to 22 months, the longest of any animal.

q: Which is the largest living rodent?
fact: The capybara is the largest living rodent.

q: Which is the largest living lizard?
fact: Komodo dragons can reach about 3 m (10 ft) and 150 kg (330 lb).

q: Which is the world's largest living bird?
fact: The ostrich is the heaviest and largest living bird.

q: How do honeybees tell hive-mates where flowers are?
fact: The waggle dance shows direction and distance to food, water or new nest sites.

q: What does a camel's hump mainly store?
fact: The humps are reservoirs of fatty tissue used as a calorie reserve, not water.

q: About how far can an owl turn its head?
fact: Owls can rotate their heads and necks as much as 270 degrees.

q: How do dolphins sleep?
fact: Dolphins sleep with only half the brain at a time, staying alert for days on end.

q: A cow's stomach has how many compartments?
fact: Cattle have one large stomach with four compartments: rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum.

q: 'Hippopotamus' comes from Greek words meaning what?
fact: Hippopotamus comes from the Ancient Greek for 'horse of the river'.

q: Which is the largest living fish?
fact: The whale shark is the largest known living fish species.

q: Wild penguins live almost entirely in which part of the world?
fact: Penguins live almost exclusively in the Southern Hemisphere; none live in the Arctic.

q: An alligator's snout is typically what shape?
fact: Alligators have broad, U-shaped snouts; crocodile snouts are typically more pointed and V-shaped.

q: What colour is an adult polar bear's skin?
fact: Polar bears have black skin under their fur, which helps absorb warmth.

q: Which body part does a butterfly use to taste a leaf?
fact: Butterflies have chemoreceptors on their feet that act like taste buds.

q: A group of crows is called a what?
fact: The collective name for a group of crows is a murder.

q: A group of lions is called a what?
fact: A group of lions living together is called a pride.

q: Koalas mostly munch the leaves of which tree?
fact: Most of a koala's diet is eucalyptus leaves.

q: Giant pandas get about 99% of their diet from what?
fact: About 99% of a giant panda's diet is bamboo, despite being classed as a carnivore.

q: A baby horse is called a what?
fact: A foal is a young horse or other equine up to one year old.

q: How many legs do adult spiders have?
fact: Adult arachnids, spiders included, have eight legs; insects have six.

q: What are shark skeletons made of?
fact: Sharks have skeletons of cartilage, which is lighter and more flexible than bone.

q: Domestic dogs are descended from which animal?
fact: Dogs are domesticated descendants of an ancient, extinct wolf population.

q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
fact: An octopus has a main heart plus two gill hearts.

q: Which planet is the hottest in our solar system?
fact: Venus's thick atmosphere traps heat, hot enough to melt lead (about 467 C), even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.

q: Which planet is less dense than water, so it would float in a big enough bathtub?
fact: NASA says Saturn is the only planet in our solar system with an average density lower than water.

q: Which planet spins tipped on its side, its equator nearly at a right angle to its orbit?
fact: Uranus is tilted about 98 degrees, so it appears to roll around the Sun on its side.

q: Which planet is the farthest from the Sun?
fact: Neptune is the eighth and most distant planet, about 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth is.

q: About how much of the solar system's total mass is the Sun?
fact: NASA says the Sun holds 99.8% of the solar system's mass. Everything else is leftovers.

q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
fact: Mercury orbits at an average of about 36 million miles from the Sun and circles it every 88 days.

q: The Moon's surface gravity is about what fraction of Earth's?
fact: Moon gravity is one-sixth of Earth's, which is why Apollo astronauts bounced along the surface.

q: Which is the biggest planet in our solar system?
fact: NASA calls Jupiter the largest planet in the solar system: about 1,000 Earths could fit inside it.

q: Since 2006, how has Pluto officially been classed?
fact: In 2006 the IAU's new planet definition demoted Pluto to a dwarf planet, leaving eight planets.

q: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
fact: NASA says it takes about eight minutes for light from the Sun to reach Earth.

q: What was the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth?
fact: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik on October 4, 1957, starting the Space Age.

q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
fact: Armstrong stepped onto the Moon on July 20, 1969, during Apollo 11. Aldrin followed him out.

q: Who was the first human to travel into space?
fact: Gagarin flew aboard Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961 and orbited Earth once.

q: Who was the first woman in space?
fact: Tereshkova flew Vostok 6 on 16 June 1963, aged 26, with the call sign 'Chaika' (seagull).

q: Who became the first American in space, in 1961?
fact: Shepard flew a 15-minute suborbital hop in Freedom 7 on May 5, 1961. Glenn was the first American to orbit.

q: Which spacecraft was the first to exit the heliosphere and enter interstellar space?
fact: NASA says Voyager 1, launched in 1977, became the first to leave the heliosphere on Aug. 25, 2012.

q: About how often does Halley's Comet return to our skies?
fact: Halley's orbit averages 76 years. Its last visit was 1986 and it is due back around 2061.

q: What is the closest large galaxy to our Milky Way?
fact: NASA says Andromeda is the closest large galaxy to the Milky Way, about 2.5 million light-years away.

q: About how many days pass from one new Moon to the next?
fact: NASA says the lunar phase cycle takes about 29.5 days, a bit longer than the Moon's 27.3-day orbit.

q: What blocks the Sun's light during a solar eclipse?
fact: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth and casts a shadow on us.

q: Which planet takes longer to spin once on its axis than to go around the Sun?
fact: A Venus day (one spin) is 243 Earth days, longer than its 225-day year.

q: What gives Mars its reddish colour?
answers: Rusty iron minerals in its dust
fact: NASA says iron minerals in Martian dirt oxidize, or rust, making the surface look red.

q: Which gas makes up most of the air we breathe on Earth?
fact: Earth's atmosphere is 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with 1% other gases.

q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
fact: Au comes from the Latin word 'aurum' for gold. Ag is silver.

q: What is the chemical formula for common table salt?
fact: Table salt is sodium chloride, one sodium ion for every chloride ion.

q: Which element is the lightest of all?
fact: Hydrogen, with one proton and one electron, is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe.

q: Which metal is liquid at normal room temperature?
fact: Mercury is the only metallic element known to be liquid at standard temperature and pressure.

q: Which natural material sits at the top of the Mohs hardness scale?
fact: Diamond is 10 on the Mohs scale, the hardest naturally occurring material.

q: Absolute zero, the coldest possible temperature, is how many degrees Celsius?
fact: Zero kelvin is -273.15 C. The -459.67 figure is the same temperature in Fahrenheit.

q: Roughly how fast does light travel through a vacuum?
fact: Light moves at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, close to 300,000 km/s.

q: On the pH scale, what number is neutral pure water?
fact: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 with 7 neutral, which is where pure water sits.

q: Why can't you hear explosions in the vacuum of space?
answers: Space is too cold for sound
Sound travels too fast to hear
There's no air to carry sound
fact: Sound is a mechanical wave and cannot propagate through a vacuum, since there is no medium.

q: Compared with the Sun's surface, how hot is the air around a lightning bolt?
fact: The NWS says lightning can heat the air to 50,000 F, about 5 times hotter than the Sun's surface.

q: What actually makes the booming sound of thunder?
fact: Lightning rapidly heats the air, which expands violently and creates the sound wave we hear as thunder.

q: Which scale rates a tornado's strength from 0 to 5?
fact: The NWS uses the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale, which rates tornadoes from zero to five by damage.

q: Which scale rates hurricanes from Category 1 to 5 by wind speed?
fact: The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale rates hurricanes 1 to 5 using maximum sustained winds.

q: How many legs does an adult insect have?
fact: Insects have a three-part body and three pairs of jointed legs. Eight legs means spider.

q: What green pigment lets plants absorb sunlight for photosynthesis?
fact: Plants absorb light with chlorophyll, which reflects green light and so makes most plants look green.

q: A caterpillar changes into a butterfly during which life stage?
fact: During the pupal stage, adult structures form while larval ones break down. A butterfly's pupa is a chrysalis.

q: Which part of a cell makes most of its chemical energy?
fact: NHGRI: mitochondria generate most of the chemical energy needed to power the cell's reactions.

q: Which blood cells carry oxygen around the body?
fact: Red blood cells use hemoglobin to deliver oxygen from the lungs to body tissues.

q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
fact: The heart has two upper chambers (atria) and two lower chambers (ventricles).

q: About how many bones does a typical adult human have?
fact: Cleveland Clinic: adults have between 206 and 213 bones. Babies start with more, then some fuse.

q: What is the longest bone in the human body?
fact: The femur, or thigh bone, is the longest and biggest bone in the body.

q: Which tiny ear bone is the smallest in the human body?
fact: The stapes is only a few millimetres across, about 3.5 mm long, and is the body's smallest bone.

q: What is the largest organ of the human body?
fact: The skin is the largest organ in the body, covering its entire external surface.

q: How many teeth do most adults have, wisdom teeth included?
fact: Most adults have 32 permanent teeth, wisdom teeth included.

q: How many chromosomes are in a typical human body cell?
fact: Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes plus one pair of sex chromosomes, for a total of 46.

q: What shape is a DNA molecule?
fact: DNA is two strands wound around each other in a shape known as a double helix.

q: Which vitamin does your skin make when sunlight hits it?
fact: When exposed to sunlight, the skin makes a compound that the liver and kidneys convert to vitamin D.

q: What is the capital city of Australia?
fact: Canberra, not Sydney or Melbourne, is Australia's capital.

q: Which river flows through the middle of Paris?
fact: The Seine flows through Paris on its way to the English Channel at Le Havre.

q: Which is the largest ocean on Earth?
fact: The Pacific covers about 32% of the planet's total surface area.

q: The ancient Inca citadel of Machu Picchu sits in the mountains of which country?
fact: Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca citadel in southern Peru, around 2,430 m up.

q: In which Indian city is the Taj Mahal?
fact: Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in Agra as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

q: Which mountain has the highest peak above sea level on Earth?
fact: Everest rises about 8,849 m above sea level in the Himalayas.

q: Africa's tallest mountain, Kilimanjaro, rises in which country?
fact: Kilimanjaro, at 5,895 m, is the highest mountain in Africa and stands in Tanzania.

q: What is the main design in the middle of Japan's flag?
fact: Japan's flag, the Hinomaru, is a red sun disc on white.

q: Which type of leaf appears in the middle of Canada's flag?
fact: Canada's flag has one red 11-pointed maple leaf on a white band.

q: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States?
fact: The statue was a gift from the people of France, designed by Frédéric Bartholdi.

q: Which river carved the Grand Canyon?
fact: The Colorado River cut the Grand Canyon in Arizona.

q: The Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system, is off the coast of which country?
fact: It is located in the Coral Sea off Queensland, Australia.

q: The Panama Canal links the Pacific Ocean with which other ocean?
fact: The canal joins the Pacific to the Caribbean Sea, which is part of the Atlantic.

q: The island nation of the Maldives sits in which ocean?
fact: The Maldives lie in the Indian Ocean, near the Arabian Sea.

q: How many US presidents are carved into Mount Rushmore?
fact: Washington, Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Lincoln, each about 60 feet tall.

q: Which lake holds the title of the deepest lake in the world?
fact: Siberia's Lake Baikal is about 1,642 m deep at its maximum.

q: What is the smallest country in the world by area?
fact: Vatican City covers only about 0.49 square kilometres.

q: What is the largest island in the world (not counting continents)?
fact: Greenland is the world's largest island that is not a continent.

q: The Strait of Gibraltar separates Europe from which continent?
fact: The narrow strait links the Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea and separates Europe from Africa.

q: What is the capital city of Brazil?
fact: Brasília was founded in 1960 and replaced Rio de Janeiro as Brazil's capital.

q: Which city is Switzerland's official 'federal city' and seat of government?
fact: Swiss lawmakers chose Bern as the Federal City in 1848.

q: Which river flows through Cairo and then spreads into a delta on the Mediterranean?
fact: The Nile passes Cairo, then forms a delta before reaching the Mediterranean Sea.

q: Angel Falls, the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall, drops in which country?
fact: Angel Falls in Venezuela's Canaima National Park is 979 m high.

q: Which Wonder of the Ancient World is the only one still largely standing today?
fact: The Great Pyramid, built around 2600 BC, is the only ancient wonder that remains largely intact.

q: The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, helped scholars crack which ancient writing?
fact: Its decree appears in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, and Champollion used it to decode Egyptian script.

q: Who led the 1922 dig that found the tomb of Tutankhamun?
fact: Howard Carter and his patron Lord Carnarvon found the boy king's tomb in 1922.

q: Whose expedition made the first voyage around the world, from 1519 to 1522?
fact: Magellan died on the way; Juan Sebastián Elcano finished the trip and returned to Spain.

q: In which country is the prehistoric stone circle of Stonehenge?
fact: Stonehenge stands in Wiltshire, England, and was built in phases from about 3100 BC.

q: The Parthenon, a temple on the Acropolis in Athens, was dedicated to which goddess?
fact: The Parthenon was built in the 5th century BC for Athena, patron goddess of Athens.

q: The Colosseum in Rome was best known for hosting what?
fact: Opened in AD 80, it held gladiator contests, animal hunts and other public spectacles.

q: The Terracotta Army of clay soldiers guards the tomb of which Chinese emperor?
fact: Farmers digging a well near Xi'an found the army in 1974, buried near Qin Shi Huang's tomb.

q: In what year did Christopher Columbus's first voyage reach the Americas?
fact: Columbus landed in the Caribbean on 12 October 1492 on a Spanish-backed voyage.

q: Portuguese sailor Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa to reach which country in 1498?
fact: Da Gama landed at Calicut (Kozhikode), opening a sea route between Europe and India.

q: What name did Norse explorer Leif Erikson give to the grape-filled land he found?
fact: Leif named it Vinland, meaning Wineland, after wild vines and grapes.

q: The original Olympic Games of ancient Greece were held at which site?
fact: The ancient games were held at Olympia to honour Zeus, traditionally starting in 776 BC.

q: 'Mesopotamia' means 'land between' which two rivers?
fact: Mesopotamia lay between the Tigris and Euphrates, where the Sumerians developed cuneiform.

q: Which civilization built the pyramid El Castillo at Chichen Itza in Mexico?
fact: Chichen Itza was a Maya city; its main pyramid is the Temple of Kukulcán, El Castillo.

q: The Great Sphinx of Giza has the body of which animal?
fact: The Sphinx is a limestone statue with a human head and a lion's body.

q: Explorer Marco Polo, who traveled to the court of Kublai Khan, came from which Italian city?
fact: Marco Polo was born in Venice around 1254 and wrote about his Asian travels.

q: In what year did the Wright brothers make the first powered airplane flight?
fact: On 17 December 1903 at Kitty Hawk, Orville's first flight lasted 12 seconds.

q: Around 1440, Johannes Gutenberg developed what in Europe?
fact: Gutenberg's press printed his famous 42-line Bible by 1455.

q: Who invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN?
fact: Berners-Lee proposed the Web in March 1989 at CERN and built the first browser and server.

q: Which scientist discovered penicillin in 1928 after spotting mould on a dish?
fact: Fleming saw mould had destroyed bacteria around it on a culture plate.

q: In 1867, Alfred Nobel patented which explosive?
fact: Nobel's dynamite was safer than nitroglycerin; his will later founded the Nobel Prizes.

q: As a teenager in 1820s Paris, who devised a raised-dot reading system for blind people?
fact: Braille presented his system at 15 in 1825 while a student at a Paris school for blind youth.

q: Edward Jenner's 1796 cowpox vaccine protected people against which disease?
fact: Jenner inoculated eight-year-old James Phipps with cowpox in 1796 to guard against smallpox.

q: What stuck to his dog's fur and inspired George de Mestral to invent Velcro?
fact: Burs' tiny hooks caught on loops of fur and clothing, inspiring Velcro's hook-and-loop design.

q: What melted in his pocket near a radar set and led Percy Spencer to the microwave oven?
fact: Working on radar magnetrons at Raytheon, Spencer's candy bar melted; he then tested popcorn.

q: In 1800, Alessandro Volta invented the first what?
fact: Volta's voltaic pile made a steady electric current; the volt is named after him.

q: Hungarian editor László Bíró made which writing tool practical in the 1930s?
fact: Bíró patented a ball-and-socket pen in 1938; it became the first commercially successful ballpoint.

q: What was the first product ever scanned with a UPC barcode, in 1974?
fact: On 26 June 1974 a 10-pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit was scanned in Troy, Ohio.

q: What did Thomas Edison invent in 1877 to record and replay sound?
fact: Edison announced the tinfoil phonograph in November 1877.

q: Who was granted the first US patent for the telephone, in 1876?
fact: Bell received US patent No. 174,465 on 7 March 1876.

q: French doctor René Laennec rolled up paper in 1816 and ended up inventing what?
fact: Laennec used rolled paper to hear heartbeats without pressing his ear to a patient's chest.

q: Which ancient civilization is traditionally credited with inventing paper?
fact: Paper-making is credited to Cai Lun of China's Han dynasty, traditionally in 105 CE.

q: Who directed the 1975 shark thriller Jaws?
fact: Steven Spielberg directed Jaws, released in 1975.

q: Which 1995 film was the first entirely computer-animated feature film?
fact: Pixar's Toy Story (1995), directed by John Lasseter, was the first fully computer-animated feature.

q: In Gone with the Wind, who says "Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn"?
fact: Rhett Butler (Clark Gable) says it as he walks away from Scarlett at the end of the 1939 film.

q: In Citizen Kane, what is "Rosebud" revealed to be?
fact: The film ends as Kane's staff burn the sled he played on as a boy; it has the name Rosebud on it.

q: What type of car is the time machine in Back to the Future?
fact: Doc Brown's time machine is a DeLorean that must hit 88 mph to travel through time.

q: In E.T., which candy does Elliott use to lure the alien out of hiding?
fact: Elliott leaves a trail of Reese's Pieces to lead E.T. into his house in the 1982 film.

q: What is the name of Dorothy's dog in The Wizard of Oz?
fact: Dorothy's little dog Toto was played by a cairn terrier named Terry in the 1939 film.

q: In The Lion King, what is the name of Simba's father?
fact: Mufasa is king of the Pride Lands and father of Simba; his brother Scar is the villain.

q: Who directed the 1997 movie Titanic?
fact: James Cameron directed Titanic, which won the Oscar for Best Picture at the 70th Academy Awards.

q: In Jurassic Park, dinosaur DNA is found in a mosquito preserved in what?
fact: The film's scientists extract dinosaur DNA from prehistoric mosquitoes trapped in amber.

q: In the 1933 film King Kong, which building does Kong climb at the end?
fact: Kong climbs the Empire State Building before being shot down by airplanes.

q: What is the name of the computer in the 1968 film 2001: A Space Odyssey?
fact: Stanley Kubrick's 2001 features HAL 9000, the spaceship Discovery's computer.

q: The Sound of Music (1965) is set in which country?
fact: The film is set in Salzburg, Austria, and follows the seven von Trapp children.

q: In Finding Nemo, what kind of fish is Nemo?
fact: Nemo and his father Marlin are clownfish; Dory is a regal blue tang.

q: In Mary Poppins, what does the nanny use to float down from the sky?
fact: In the 1964 film, Mary Poppins descends from the clouds holding her umbrella.

q: Which film won the very first Academy Award for Best Animated Feature?
fact: Shrek won the inaugural Best Animated Feature Oscar at the 74th Academy Awards.

q: Who is Pinocchio's conscience in Disney's 1940 film?
fact: Jiminy Cricket, voiced by Cliff Edwards, is Pinocchio's conscience and sings "When You Wish Upon a Star."

q: In The Flintstones, what is the name of the town where the family lives?
fact: The cartoon is set in the Stone Age town of Bedrock.

q: What breed of dog is Scooby-Doo?
fact: Scooby-Doo, Where Are You! debuted in 1969, starring a Great Dane and his friends.

q: On Sesame Street, where does Oscar the Grouch live?
fact: Oscar the Grouch lives in a trash can on Sesame Street, which first aired in 1969.

q: In the original 1960s Star Trek, Captain Kirk commands which starship?
fact: James T. Kirk (William Shatner) is captain of the USS Enterprise in Star Trek, which began in 1966.

q: Which cartoon rabbit's catchphrase is "What's up, Doc?"
fact: Bugs Bunny, voiced originally by Mel Blanc, debuted in 1940 and loves carrots.

q: Who is the frog host of The Muppet Show?
fact: Kermit the Frog hosted and ran the variety show, which aired from 1976 to 1981.

q: On The Simpsons, Homer works as a safety inspector at what?
fact: Homer is a safety inspector at the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant.

q: In which decade did the cartoon Tom and Jerry first appear?
fact: William Hanna and Joseph Barbera created Tom and Jerry in 1940.

q: How many keys does a standard modern piano have?
fact: A standard piano has 52 white keys and 36 black keys, for 88 in total.

q: How many strings does a standard violin have?
fact: A violin has four strings, normally tuned G, D, A and E in perfect fifths.

q: In which English city did The Beatles form?
fact: The Beatles formed in Liverpool in 1960 and broke up in 1970.

q: Michael Jackson's 1982 album with "Billie Jean" and "Beat It" is called what?
fact: Thriller was released on November 29, 1982 and includes both "Billie Jean" and "Beat It."

q: Which band recorded "Bohemian Rhapsody" on the 1975 album A Night at the Opera?
fact: Freddie Mercury wrote "Bohemian Rhapsody" for Queen; it runs 5 minutes 55 seconds.

q: Though often made of brass, the saxophone belongs to which instrument family?
fact: The sax is a single-reed woodwind with a conical body, invented by Belgian Adolphe Sax.

q: In which city was composer Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart born?
fact: Mozart was born in Salzburg, Austria, on January 27, 1756.

q: The pop group ABBA, known for "Dancing Queen," came from which country?
fact: ABBA formed in Stockholm in 1972 and won Eurovision in 1974 with "Waterloo."

q: Which brass instrument is famous for its long telescoping slide?
fact: Nearly all trombones use a telescoping slide, instead of valves, to change pitch.

q: Which standard orchestral string instrument is the largest and lowest-pitched?
fact: The double bass is the largest and lowest-pitched chordophone in the modern symphony orchestra.

q: Which former Beatle released the 1971 song "Imagine"?
fact: John Lennon released "Imagine" on October 11, 1971, on the album of the same name.

q: Who composed the violin concertos known as The Four Seasons?
fact: Italian composer Antonio Vivaldi's Four Seasons was published in 1725 as four violin concertos.

q: Which famous composer kept composing music even after he went deaf?
fact: Beethoven's hearing loss began around 1798, yet he went on to write his Ninth Symphony in 1824.

q: How high above the floor is a regulation basketball rim?
fact: The rim sits exactly 10 feet (3.05 m) above the court.

q: What did James Naismith nail up as the first basketball goals?
fact: Naismith nailed peach baskets to an elevated track in Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1891.

q: A full marathon race is about how far?
fact: The marathon distance was set at 42.195 km (26 miles 385 yards) in 1921, after the 1908 London Olympics.

q: How many interlocking rings are in the Olympic symbol?
fact: The five rings, designed in 1913, represent the union of the five continents.

q: Which city hosted the first modern Summer Olympics in 1896?
fact: The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens, Greece, in April 1896.

q: In baseball, how many strikes make a batter strike out?
fact: A batter against whom three strikes are recorded strikes out; four balls earns a walk.

q: In golf, a birdie is a score of how many strokes relative to par?
fact: A birdie is one stroke under par; an eagle is two under and a bogey one over.

q: In tennis scoring, what does "love" mean?
fact: "Love" is the tennis term for zero points.

q: How many players does a soccer team have on the field, including the goalkeeper?
fact: Association football is played by two teams of 11 players each.

q: How many points is a touchdown worth in American football?
fact: A touchdown scores 6 points; the extra point after it adds 1 or a two-point conversion adds 2.

q: What do ice hockey players hit with their sticks?
fact: Hockey uses a puck made of vulcanized rubber, hit toward the opponent's goal.

q: Which Grand Slam tennis tournament is still played on grass?
fact: Wimbledon is the only tennis major still played on grass.

q: Who scored the first perfect 10 in Olympic gymnastics, at the 1976 Games?
fact: At age 14 in Montreal, Comaneci's perfect score showed as "1.00" because the board couldn't display 10.

q: What color jersey is worn by the overall leader of the Tour de France?
fact: The yellow jersey honors the yellow paper of L'Auto, the newspaper that created the race in 1903.

q: How many strikes in a row make a perfect 300 game in ten-pin bowling?
fact: A perfect game of 300 takes twelve consecutive strikes.

q: What was volleyball originally called when William G. Morgan invented it in 1895?
fact: Morgan, a YMCA director in Holyoke, Massachusetts, called it Mintonette before it was renamed volleyball.

q: In baseball, how far is the pitcher's plate from home plate?
fact: The pitching distance of 60 feet 6 inches was set in 1893.

q: What is the hardest substance your body makes?
fact: Enamel is about 96% mineral, more than any other tissue you make. Chomp responsibly.

q: Fresh sweat barely smells. What makes you stink?
fact: Sweat is colorless and odorless until skin bacteria break it down.

q: Pus is mostly made of dead what?
fact: Pus is mainly dead white blood cells (plus dead bacteria) left from the immune fight.

q: What gives poop its brown color?
fact: Old red blood cells make bilirubin, which gut bacteria turn into stercobilin, the brown pigment.

q: How do head lice get from head to head?
answers: They crawl; no hopping or flying
fact: The CDC says head lice move by crawling; they cannot hop or fly.

q: What are the 'nits' stuck to hair in a lice outbreak?
fact: Nits are lice eggs, laid close to the scalp; they hatch in about a week.

q: What causes common warts?
fact: Warts are skin growths caused by infection with the human papillomavirus.

q: Athlete's foot is an infection caused by what?
fact: Fungi such as Trichophyton rubrum cause it; roughly 15% of people have it at any time.

q: You swallow a piece of chewing gum. What happens to it?
fact: Gum is indigestible but just gets pushed along and exits; the 7-year claim is folklore.

q: Where does the gas in a typical burp come from?
fact: Swallowed air (or carbon dioxide from fizzy drinks) that can't be absorbed gets burped out.

q: Why does your nose run when you cry?
fact: Extra tears flow through the nasolacrimal duct into the nasal cavity.

q: Where does most of the snot your nose makes end up?
fact: Cilia sweep mucus to the throat, and most of it is swallowed without you noticing.

q: How much mucus do experts think your body makes daily?
fact: Cleveland Clinic: most experts think the body makes about a liter of mucus a day.

q: Dust mites chow down mostly on what?
fact: House dust mites feed on skin flakes from humans and other animals.

q: What causes the itchy skin condition scabies?
fact: CDC: the microscopic scabies mite burrows into the upper layer of skin and lays eggs.

q: The crusty 'sleep' in your eye corners has what proper name?
fact: Rheum is dried mucus, skin cells, blood cells and dust that collects around the eyes.

q: Earwax is partly made by modified what?
fact: Ceruminous glands are modified sweat glands; sebaceous glands add oily sebum.

q: Wet or dry earwax: what decides which you get?
fact: Wet wax is dominant and dry is recessive, tied to the ABCC11 gene.

q: What mainly causes bad breath?
fact: Tongue bacteria make smelly sulfur compounds and cause most mouth-related bad breath.

q: What turns the sugar you eat into tooth-eating acid?
fact: NIDCR: decay-causing bacteria meeting sugars and starches form acid that wears enamel.

q: The sticky film dentists scrape off your teeth is mostly what?
fact: Dental plaque is a biofilm of microorganisms, mostly bacteria.

q: Which acid does your stomach make to break down food?
fact: Stomach cells make hydrochloric acid, with a pH of about 1 to 3.

q: What keeps stomach acid from eating the stomach itself?
fact: The stomach lining secretes mucus and bicarbonate that shield it from the acid.

q: Hair and fingernails are made of the same protein. Which?
fact: Fingernails and toenails are made of alpha-keratin; hair is mainly keratin proteins too.

q: How fast does scalp hair grow on average?
fact: Hair is commonly said to grow about 1 cm per month, with wide variation.

q: Fingernails vs toenails: which grow faster, and how much?
answers: They grow at the same speed
fact: Fingernails grow about 3.5 mm a month versus about 1.6 mm for toenails.

q: Lose a toenail and it takes about how long to regrow?
fact: Fingernails regrow in 3 to 6 months, but toenails need a year to a year and a half.

q: A 10-second kiss swaps about how many bacteria?
fact: A Dutch study in the journal Microbiome estimated about 80 million bacteria transfer.

q: Scientists swabbed 60 belly buttons. How many bacteria species turned up?
fact: The Belly Button Biodiversity project found 2,368 species, 1,458 possibly new to science.

q: What's the medical word for your tummy rumbling?
fact: Borborygmi are rumbles from gas and fluid moving through the gut, hungry or not.

q: What share of fart gas is actually the smelly stuff?
fact: Over 99% is odorless gas; the smell comes from a sliver of volatile sulfur compounds.

q: Which two gases can make a fart flammable?
fact: Hydrogen and methane in flatus are flammable. Do not test this at home.

q: Why do beans make people gassy?
answers: They are full of trapped air
fact: Bacteria in the large intestine ferment beans' carbs and release gas as a byproduct.

q: Which pigment makes pee yellow?
fact: Urobilin (urochrome) forms when colorless urobilinogen, from broken-down blood, oxidizes.

q: Spit is about what percent water?
fact: Human saliva is around 99% water, plus enzymes, mucus and some cells.

q: Your saliva starts breaking down which food type?
fact: The enzyme amylase in saliva begins digesting starch right in your mouth.

q: What tiny critters live in the eyelash follicles of most adults?
fact: Up to 90% of adults carry Demodex mites in facial hair follicles, eyelashes included.

q: Doctors sometimes put live maggots on wounds to do what?
fact: Medical maggots are FDA-approved: they liquefy and eat dead tissue, cleaning the wound.

q: Doctors treat some stubborn gut infections with a transplant of what?
fact: Fecal transplants move gut microbes from a healthy donor and cure most C. diff cases.

q: Tonsil stones are mostly bacteria plus what?
fact: They are biofilms of bacteria with calcium salts, trapped in tonsil crevices.

q: A hairball in a human stomach is called a what?
fact: Digestion can't break down hair, so swallowed hair can pile up into a trichobezoar.

q: What gives green snot its color?
answers: An enzyme from white blood cells
fact: Neutrophils release myeloperoxidase, a green heme enzyme, into mucus.

q: Foot odor is partly caused by a bacterium that also ripens what?
fact: Brevibacterium linens lives on skin and helps ripen Limburger and Munster cheese.

q: A newborn's very first poop, dark and tar-like, is called?
fact: Meconium is sticky, dark olive stool made of stuff the baby swallowed in the womb.

q: Newborns are often coated in a waxy white layer called what?
fact: Vernix caseosa is mostly water with lipids and proteins, plus sebum and shed skin cells.

q: The sweat that cools you off is mostly made of what?
fact: Eccrine sweat is clear, odorless and 98-99% water.

q: What makes a blackhead black?
fact: Plugged-pore contents react with air and darken; it is not about being unclean.

q: How long can a beef tapeworm grow inside a person?
fact: The CDC says Taenia saginata tapeworms can reach up to 10 meters in length.

q: What shape is a wombat's poop?
fact: Wombat intestines mold dry poop into cubes, which stack on rocks and logs without rolling away.

q: A bare-nosed wombat may drop up to how many poop cubes a day?
fact: Bare-nosed wombats poop four to eight pieces at a time and may make up to 100 cubes a day.

q: How often does a three-toed sloth climb down its tree to poop?
fact: Three-toed sloths descend roughly once a week to defecate, a risky trip that benefits the moths in their fur.

q: Moths live in a sloth's fur, and what green stuff grows there that sloths may snack on?
fact: Sloth-fur moths and the algae they help fertilize form a garden that supplements the sloth's leafy diet.

q: Why do vultures poop on their own legs?
fact: Called urohidrosis: droppings on the legs evaporate and cool the bird.

q: When threatened, turkey vultures may fire what at attackers?
fact: Turkey vultures puke stinging acid at predators, which also lightens them for a quick getaway.

q: What does a hagfish do to a predator that bites it?
fact: Hagfish slime fills a predator's mouth and gills, making it gag and back off.

q: How does a hagfish scrape its own slime off its body?
answers: Peels it off with its claws
fact: A hagfish knots its body and slides the knot down to wipe away slime so it doesn't suffocate itself.

q: At night, African dung beetles steer their dung balls in a straight line using what?
fact: A 2013 study showed dung beetles use the Milky Way's glow to roll straight, a first for any animal.

q: The horned dung beetle Onthophagus taurus can pull how many times its own body weight?
fact: Its pulling record is 1,141 times body weight, like a person hauling six double-decker buses.

q: Why do rabbits re-eat their own special soft droppings?
fact: Eating cecotropes gives rabbits a second pass at nutrients from fibrous plants.

q: Baby koalas eat 'pap' from their mother to pick up what?
fact: Pap is full of live bacteria that help a joey's gut handle eucalyptus leaves when it stops drinking milk.

q: A horned lizard defends itself by squirting what out of its eyes?
fact: Horned lizards can squirt an aimed stream of blood from the corners of the eyes up to 5 feet.

q: The northern fulmar defends itself by projectile-vomiting what?
fact: Fulmars shoot a stream of stomach oil up to about six feet, which ruins other birds' feathers.

q: What can a stressed sea cucumber do with its insides?
answers: Spew them out and regrow them
fact: Sea cucumbers can eject their guts to escape, then regrow the digestive tract in weeks.

q: The tongue-eating louse does what to a snapper's tongue?
fact: Cymothoa exigua cuts off the tongue's blood supply, then attaches itself to the stub as a replacement.

q: How do vampire bats help a hungry roostmate?
fact: Vampire bats regurgitate blood to feed starving roostmates, even unrelated ones.

q: Scientists can spot hidden Antarctic penguin colonies from space by looking for what?
fact: Dense colonies leave pink guano stains, coloured by their krill diet, visible in satellite images.

q: The red 'blood sweat' of hippos is really what?
fact: It is neither blood nor sweat but red and orange pigments that block UV and slow bacteria.

q: What might a housefly do after landing on your sandwich?
answers: Weave a silk web over it
fact: Flies can regurgitate stored crop contents right onto your bread.

q: Houseflies taste food with their what?
fact: Houseflies have taste receptors on their legs, so they identify food by walking on it.

q: How hot can a bombardier beetle's defensive spray get?
fact: The beetle mixes two chemicals in a rear chamber and blasts out a spray up to about 100°C.

q: The FDA cleared blood-sucking leeches in 2004 to help with what?
fact: Leeches remove pooled blood under skin grafts and restore circulation in blocked veins.

q: To digest a clam, many starfish push their what out of their body?
fact: Many starfish evert their stomach to digest prey outside the body.

q: How do spiders eat prey without chewing?
fact: Spiders spit digestive juices onto prey, then suck up the liquefied meal.

q: Frogs use which body part to help push food down their throat?
fact: Frogs retract their eyes into the mouth to push prey toward the esophagus.

q: How long can a cockroach live without its head?
fact: Headless roaches can live for weeks because they breathe through body spiracles and barely bleed.

q: How do owls get rid of bones and fur they can't digest?
answers: Poop them out in a pile
fact: Owls regurgitate indigestible bones, teeth and fur as a compact pellet, often at roost.

q: Pigeon 'milk' for chicks is produced in what part of the parent?
fact: Fluid-filled cells from the lining of the crop are shed to make protein-rich pigeon milk.

q: Lobsters pee out of which part of their body?
fact: Lobsters have bladders in their heads and release urine plumes to signal rivals and mates.

q: Archerfish knock insects off branches by spitting what?
fact: Archerfish shoot a jet of water from a tube formed by tongue and mouth roof.

q: What do parrotfish poop out that builds tropical beaches?
fact: Parrotfish munch coral and excrete sand; they helped build Hawaiian beaches and a Maldives island.

q: In winter, how do honeybees mostly handle bathroom breaks?
fact: Bees keep making feces all winter and leave the hive to relieve themselves on warm, dry days.

q: What lives in the pores of almost every adult's face?
fact: Face mites live in hair follicles, and DNA tests found them on every adult sampled.

q: Which of these animals physically cannot vomit?
fact: Horses have a very strong esophageal sphincter and a weak vomiting reflex.

q: Most of a cow's methane comes out as what?
fact: Methane from a cow's rumen is largely burped out; very little is released at the other end.

q: Why do pigs wallow in mud?
fact: Pigs lack functional sweat glands, so they wallow in mud or water to cool off.

q: What makes bird poop white?
fact: Whitish uric acid crystals from the bird's urine give droppings their white colour.

q: Why is spotted hyena poop bright white?
fact: Hyenas crunch bones, so their droppings are loaded with calcium and phosphorus.

q: A silver-spotted skipper caterpillar can fire its poop pellets about how far?
fact: Skipper caterpillars launch frass as far as 153 cm, probably to hide from predators.

q: A snail's ribbon-like tongue is lined with thousands of tiny what?
fact: Snails and slugs eat with a jaw and a radula, a band of thousands of microscopic teeth.

q: Which large seabird do Galapagos vampire finches prick for a blood meal?
fact: Vampire ground finches peck booby skin and drink the blood, especially when food is scarce.

q: Ambergris, a perfume ingredient, forms in the gut of which animal?
fact: Ambergris forms in the sperm whale's intestines and is passed out like faecal matter.

q: Some pearlfish hide from predators inside the rear end of what?
fact: Some pearlfish species live inside a sea cucumber's anus for shelter.

q: New World tarantulas defend themselves by flinging what from their abdomen?
fact: They rub their hind legs on the abdomen to throw irritating urticating hairs at attackers.

q: A skunk's stinky spray comes from glands near its what?
fact: Skunks spray sulfur-rich liquid from anal scent glands, aiming accurately up to about 3 m (10 ft).

q: Many baby termites get their gut microbes by doing what?
fact: Neonates get gut symbionts by feeding on parents' gut fluids, called proctodeal trophallaxis.

q: Sardinia's casu marzu is a cheese famous for containing live what?
fact: Cheese-fly larvae are added to pecorino and their digestion ferments it. Sale is banned in the EU.

q: Which tiny critters give France's bright orange Mimolette cheese its crusty rind?
fact: Mites munch the rind for years. The US FDA once blocked imports over a six-mites-per-square-inch limit.

q: The red food dye carmine, found in some pink yogurts, is made from what?
fact: Carmine is extracted from the dried, pulverized bodies of cochineal insects.

q: The shiny 'confectioner's glaze' on jelly beans is made from what?
fact: Shellac is a resin secreted by female lac bugs. It is also sold as confectioner's glaze.

q: What did Swiss researchers find causes the holes in Swiss cheese?
answers: Tiny bits of hay in the milk
fact: Agroscope scientists found hay particles in milk form the 'eyes'. Cleaner milking means fewer holes.

q: Why must Iceland's hákarl shark meat be fermented before anyone eats it?
fact: Fresh Greenland shark flesh is toxic (TMAO). Fermenting and drying it for months makes it edible.

q: Castoreum, a rare 'natural flavouring', comes from the glands of which animal?
fact: Beaver castoreum is FDA-approved as a flavouring but is now exceedingly rare in food.

q: Kopi luwak coffee beans have been eaten and pooped out by which animal?
fact: Civets eat the coffee cherries, and the partly digested beans are collected from their droppings.

q: Chinese bird's-nest soup is made from nests built from what?
fact: Edible-nest swiftlet nests are made entirely of solidified saliva.

q: Ancient Rome's favourite sauce, garum, was fermented from what?
fact: Romans fermented fish guts with salt for months, much like modern fish sauce.

q: How long are Chinese 'century eggs' actually preserved?
fact: Eggs are cured in clay, ash, salt and quicklime for several weeks to a few months, not a century.

q: Marmite is a spread made from leftover what from beer-making?
fact: Marmite began in 1902 using spare yeast from Bass Brewery in Burton upon Trent.

q: Natto, the stringy Japanese breakfast, is soybeans fermented with which bacterium?
fact: Cooked soybeans are fermented with Bacillus subtilis var. natto, which makes the sticky strands.

q: Sweden's notoriously stinky surströmming is canned, fermented what?
fact: Surströmming is fermented Baltic Sea herring, famous for its powerful smell when the can is opened.

q: The US FDA allows peanut butter to average up to 30 what per 100 grams?
fact: The FDA's defect action level for peanut butter is an average of 30 insect fragments per 100 g.

q: At the English royal court, what was the Groom of the Stool's job?
answers: Helping the king with the toilet
fact: The most intimate courtier helped the monarch with excretion and hygiene, and later gained real power.

q: Who is credited with building a flush toilet for Queen Elizabeth I in the 1590s?
fact: Her godson Harington installed one at Richmond Palace. Crapper came centuries later and did not invent the toilet.

q: During London's Great Stink of 1858, Parliament soaked its curtains in what?
fact: Parliament doused its curtains in chloride of lime to mask the Thames reek, then passed a law within 18 days.

q: What was a Roman 'vomitorium' actually?
answers: A room to purge after feasts
A passage for crowds to exit
fact: Vomitoria were stadium passages that 'spewed' crowds out. The puking-room idea is a modern myth.

q: Emperor Vespasian's line 'money does not stink' defended a tax on what?
fact: Vespasian taxed urine collection and held up coins to ask Titus if they smelled. 'Pecunia non olet' became a proverb.

q: George Washington's dentures were not wooden. One set had carved what?
fact: One set was made of carved hippo ivory, human teeth and brass nails. The wood myth came from stains.

q: Where was toilet paper first written about, around the year 589?
fact: Scholar Yan Zhitui wrote about it in 589, so paper was used for hygiene in China by the 6th century.

q: 'Mellitus' in diabetes mellitus comes from the Latin for what, after sweet urine?
fact: Doctors tasted urine to diagnose diabetes. 'Mellitus' comes from the Latin for honey, hence 'honey-sweet'.

q: For thousands of years, people blamed toothaches on what?
fact: A Babylonian tablet, 'The Legend of the Worm', blames tooth worms. The belief lasted into the 18th century.

q: What valuable item did Samuel Pepys famously bury in his garden in the Great Fire of 1666?
fact: Pepys hid his valuables and famously buried a round of parmesan cheese in his garden.

q: At medieval feasts, what were 'trenchers' used as?
fact: A trencher was a flat round of stale bread used as a plate, then eaten or given to the poor.

q: Old Edinburgh folk yelled 'Gardyloo!' before doing what from their windows?
fact: 'Gardyloo' came from the French for 'beware of the water'. The 1749 Nastiness Act tried to curb the practice.

q: Old-time tanners softened raw hides by working in which smelly ingredient?
fact: Bating and puering used hen, pigeon or dog droppings. Their bacterial enzymes made leather soft.

q: In Tudor England, what was a 'gong farmer's' job?
fact: Gong farmers dug out privies and cesspits, and were only allowed to work at night.

q: A brainless slime mould recreated which city's rail network in a 2010 experiment?
fact: Physarum polycephalum, fed oat flakes at city positions, grew tubes much like Tokyo's rail map.

q: Which gas gives Uranus's cloud tops a rotten-egg smell?
fact: Gemini North observations confirmed hydrogen sulfide in Uranus's cloud tops, the gas of rotten eggs.

q: Astronauts say the smell of space clinging to their suits resembles what?
fact: Spacewalkers report an acrid smell of seared steak, hot metal and welding fumes after coming inside.

q: The titan arum is nicknamed the 'corpse flower' for smelling like what?
fact: The rare bloom unleashes a stench like rotting flesh inside the greenhouse.

q: How long does a corpse flower bloom stay open before collapsing?
fact: The rare, stinky titan arum bloom lasts only about 24 to 48 hours.

q: The 'zombie-ant' fungus forces infected ants to bite what before they die?
fact: At solar noon the fungus makes ants bite a leaf's main vein, in a cool damp spot good for the fungus.

q: The earthy smell of rain comes partly from a compound made by which microbes?
fact: Soil bacteria like Streptomyces make geosmin. Humans can smell it at about 5 parts per trillion.

q: To turn nectar into honey, bees repeatedly do what with it?
fact: Foragers regurgitate nectar to hive bees, which regurgitate it into wax cells while adding enzymes.
